claims.text: The as-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an FCC matrix.
The as-built alloy contains grain boundaries, porosity, and other AM-induced defect sites.
Under reducing conditions at 750–850 K, hydrogen enters the alloy.
Hydrogen accumulates or segregates at grain boundaries, porosity, and other microstructural defects.
Hydrogen accumulation at defects reduces local cohesive or atomic bonding strength.
Hydrogen-induced loss of cohesion promotes localized embrittlement and microcrack initiation.
Hydrogen-driven defect-localized embrittlement can cause catastrophic failure of the alloy in reducing gas.
Under oxidizing conditions at 700–900 K, Ti and Cr undergo selective oxidation.
Selective oxidation produces Ti- and Cr-rich oxide precipitates along grain and sub-grain boundaries.
The boundary oxide precipitates are brittle and act as stress concentrators.
Ti- and Cr-rich boundary oxides weaken intergranular cohesion and initiate intergranular cracking.
Oxidation-driven intergranular damage can precipitate catastrophic failure.
Reducing-gas exposure will produce greater deuterium uptake than inert exposure.
Reducing-gas exposure will increase microcrack density at defect sites relative to the inert baseline.
Reducing-gas exposure will lower the mechanical failure threshold relative to the inert baseline.
Increasing oxygen partial pressure will increase the formation of Ti- and Cr-rich oxide precipitates.
Increasing oxide-precipitate formation will correlate with intergranular cracking and reduced mechanical integrity.
Inert exposure will yield minimal hydrogen uptake and oxide formation while maintaining mechanical stability.
The proposed mechanisms are applicable within 750–850 K for reducing environments and 700–900 K for oxidizing environments.
Additional degradation phenomena may become important outside the stated temperature ranges.
